---
title: "Support Vector Machines"
---

Support vector machines use margins and kernels to build classifiers
that can be linear in a transformed feature space while nonlinear in
the original inputs.

## Learning Objectives

- Explain maximal-margin classification.
- Distinguish hard-margin and soft-margin classifiers.
- Interpret support vectors and the cost parameter.
- Describe how kernels create nonlinear decision boundaries.

## Core Ideas

The SVM objective balances margin width against classification
violations. The kernel trick lets the model compute similarities in a
high-dimensional feature space without explicitly constructing every
feature.

## Separating Hyperplanes

For two classes coded as $y_i \in \{-1, 1\}$, a separating hyperplane
has the form

$$
f(x) = \beta_0 + x^\top \beta.
$$

The sign of $f(x)$ determines the predicted class. The margin is the
distance between the separating hyperplane and the closest training
points. Those closest points are the support vectors.

## Soft-Margin Classifier

Perfect separation is often impossible or undesirable. The soft-margin
classifier allows violations with slack variables:

$$
y_i(\beta_0 + x_i^\top\beta) \geq 1 - \xi_i,
\quad \xi_i \geq 0.
$$

The cost parameter controls the tradeoff between a wide margin and
classification violations. A large cost penalizes violations heavily; a
small cost allows more violations and usually a wider margin.

## Kernels

Kernels replace inner products with similarity functions. Common choices
include:

| Kernel | Use |
|---|---|
| Linear | Approximately linear class boundary |
| Polynomial | Curved boundaries with global polynomial structure |
| Radial basis | Flexible local boundaries |
| Sigmoid | Neural-network-like similarity, less common in practice |

```r
library(e1071)

linear_svm <- svm(y ~ ., data = train, kernel = "linear", cost = 1)
radial_svm <- svm(y ~ ., data = train, kernel = "radial", cost = 1)
```

SVMs are sensitive to feature scale, so numeric predictors should be
centered and scaled.

## Worked Example

Use a two-dimensional classification example to compare linear,
polynomial, and radial kernels. Show how the decision boundary changes
as the tuning parameters change.

## Applied Practice

Practice by fitting linear, radial, and polynomial SVMs after centering
and scaling numeric predictors. Tune the cost and kernel parameters
with cross-validation, then compare the resulting decision boundaries
and test-set performance.
